title: Incident management best practices for 2026: A complete guide
summary: 18 incident management best practices grouped by phase: prepare, detect, respond, communicate and learn, with a maturity model, a checklist and Rootly examples.
body_markdown:
**Incident management best practices fall into five phases.** Prepare severity levels, roles and runbooks while it’s calm. Detect with grouped alerts routed to the service owner. Respond in one channel led by a named incident commander. Communicate on a fixed cadence. Learn through retrospectives with tracked action items. In Rootly, declaring an incident opens the channel, assigns roles and starts that severity’s workflows automatically.


This guide lists 18 practices in that order. Each one gives the practice, why it matters, how to do it, and a Rootly example linked to the documentation. After the practices you’ll find a maturity model, a one-screen checklist, answers to the questions engineers ask most, and an FAQ.


## The incident management lifecycle


Every effective process moves through the same stages: **prepare → detect → respond → communicate → learn** . Triage sits inside detection, and resolution sits inside response. Treat the stages as a loop: what you learn in the retrospective should change how you prepare. The[incident response guide](https://rootly.com/incident-response) covers each stage in depth.


Phase Goal Practices Metric that shows it’s working


Prepare Decide the response before you need it 1 to 4 Share of incidents with a severity and commander in the first 5 minutes


Detect Page the right person once 5 to 7 MTTA, acknowledge rate


Respond Restore service with one coordinated effort 8 to 11 Mean time to resolve (MTTR)


Communicate Keep everyone informed without interrupting responders 12 to 14 Time to first status update


Learn Stop the same incident from coming back 15 to 18 Action-item closure, recurrence rate


## Why the old model broke: the coordination tax


Legacy alerting tools were built for one job: trigger an alarm and hand coordination to a human. That leaves responders to assemble the incident bridge by hand: spinning up a channel, pulling in the right people, opening dashboards, copying logs and filing tickets. In a typical incident, a large share of the total resolution time goes to this administrative “coordination tax” instead of the fix: assembling the team and assigning roles at the start, then cleaning up and communicating status at the end. Every practice below is about shrinking that tax so responder attention goes to diagnosis and mitigation.


## Why 2026 is a turning point: the Opsgenie sunset


The urgency to modernize has a hard deadline. Atlassian is **sunsetting standalone Opsgenie, with end of support on April 5, 2027** , pushing thousands of teams to re-evaluate their reliability stack. Many teams are using the forced migration to adopt a chat-native platform that automates the full lifecycle, instead of moving to another legacy pager or into a ticket-centric ITSM tool. If you’re migrating, treat it as a chance to fix the coordination tax as well as replace the pager.


## Phase 1: Prepare


### 1. Define a severity scale tied to a response


**Why it matters:** Severity decides who is paged, how fast, and who hears about it. A vague scale is how a SEV2 becomes a SEV1 an hour too late.


**How to do it:** Use four or five levels (for example SEV0 to SEV3). Define each one by customer impact, scope and urgency, and write down the response each level triggers. Decide in advance who sets severity; the incident commander is the usual choice.


**Rootly example:** In Rootly, each[severity](https://docs.rootly.com/configuration/severities) can be linked to Slack channels, user groups and email addresses, and workflow conditions on severity decide who is paged and when the status page is updated.


### 2. Name incident roles and write one line for each


**Why it matters:** Role clarity is the biggest driver of calm incidents. Without it, two people make conflicting calls and nobody owns the update.


**How to do it:** At minimum, name an incident commander (coordinates and decides), a communications lead (owns every update) and a technical lead per affected service. Add a scribe for long incidents. The[incident response team roles](https://rootly.com/incident-response/team-roles) guide describes each role.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[incident roles](https://docs.rootly.com/incidents/incident-roles/incident-roles) are customizable, appear in the incident sidebar, Slack and retrospectives, and workflows can assign the commander or communications lead by severity or team on-call.


### 3. Write runbooks for your top failure modes


**Why it matters:** You already know your most common incidents. A runbook stops one person from being the only one who can bring a system back.


**How to do it:** Start with the three to five services that page most. Cover the alerts that fire, the diagnostic steps and the fix, and attach a task list for the responder.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[playbooks](https://docs.rootly.com/configuration/playbooks) attach to an incident automatically when it matches a condition such as severity, service, functionality or team, and can carry tasks for the responder.


### 4. Map every service to an owner and an escalation policy


**Why it matters:** Pages that go to whoever set up an alert years ago waste the first ten minutes of every incident.


**How to do it:** Keep a service catalog with an owning team for each service. Give each team an escalation policy with a second and third step, so an unacknowledged page moves on by itself. Build fair rotations so the same people don’t carry the load.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[services](https://docs.rootly.com/configuration/services) record ownership and map to status page components, and[escalation policies](https://docs.rootly.com/on-call/escalation-policies) assigned to a team or service escalate through multi-step targets with time delays and round robin.


## Phase 2: Detect


### 5. Group and deduplicate alerts


**Why it matters:** When everything pages, nothing gets the right attention. Alert fatigue is a reliability risk, covered in detail in the[alert fatigue guide](https://rootly.com/on-call-software/alert-fatigue) .


**How to do it:** Deduplicate repeat events from the same monitor. Group alerts from different monitors that fire on the same problem. Review the noisiest monitors every month and delete or retune them.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[alert grouping](https://docs.rootly.com/alerts/alert-grouping) pages responders for one leader alert while related alerts join its group silently, and[alert deduplication](https://docs.rootly.com/alerts/alert-deduplication) collapses repeat events from one monitor into a single open alert.


### 6. Route alerts by service ownership


**Why it matters:** The fastest acknowledgement comes from paging the person who owns the failing service, first time.


**How to do it:** Route on stable alert fields (service, environment, team) instead of free-text titles, and send each route to a team, service or escalation policy.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[alert routes](https://docs.rootly.com/alerts/alert-routing) evaluate alert sources, normalized alert fields and raw payload values, then send the alert to the matching team, service or escalation policy.


### 7. Declare early and use triage for uncertain signals


**Why it matters:** Teams that wait for certainty lose the first half hour. A cheap way to declare means problems get worked sooner.


**How to do it:** Let anyone declare. Use a triage state for signals that might be real, then promote to a full incident or cancel. Record when the problem was detected and acknowledged so you can measure it.


**Rootly example:** The Rootly[incident lifecycle](https://docs.rootly.com/incidents/incident-lifecycle) has an In Triage status that limits notifications while responders confirm the issue, and records detected and acknowledged timestamps for MTTD and MTTA.


## Phase 3: Respond


### 8. Run every incident in one dedicated channel


**Why it matters:** Pulling responders into a separate tool during a SEV1 costs minutes and attention. One channel per incident gives late joiners something to read instead of questions to ask.


**How to do it:** Create a new channel for each incident in the chat tool your team already uses, name it with the severity, and keep decisions, updates and the timeline there.


**Rootly example:** In Rootly,` /rootly new` or a message action[creates an incident from Slack](https://docs.rootly.com/incidents/creating-incidents-via-slack) and opens its channel automatically. Rootly also runs incidents in[Microsoft Teams](https://docs.rootly.com/integrations/microsoft-teams) and[Google Chat](https://docs.rootly.com/integrating-with-google-chat) .


### 9. Automate the setup and keep humans on the judgment calls


**Why it matters:** Every manual setup step (channel, roles, ticket, page, status stub) is time taken from diagnosis, and a step someone forgets under pressure.


**How to do it:** Write down the first ten minutes of your response, then automate each step that doesn’t need judgment. Use conditions so the automation only runs on the incidents that need it.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[incident workflows](https://docs.rootly.com/workflows/incident-workflows) run on events such as incident created or severity updated, check run conditions, then create the channel, open Jira or ServiceNow tickets, page on-call and post status reminders.


### 10. Give the incident commander one job and hand off out loud


**Why it matters:** A commander who is also debugging stops coordinating. Silent handoffs on long incidents leave nobody sure who is in charge.


**How to do it:** The commander coordinates, sets severity and makes the calls, and does not run commands. On long incidents, announce each handoff in the channel so the timeline shows who held the role and when.


**Rootly example:** Responders assign and reassign Rootly incident roles from the incident channel, and the[incident timeline](https://docs.rootly.com/incidents/incident-timeline/incident-timeline) records role changes alongside status changes and decisions.


### 11. Mitigate first, then find the cause


**Why it matters:** Customers feel impact, not root cause. Restoring service first shortens the outage even when the cause takes days to find.


**How to do it:** Roll back, fail over or scale up first. Mark the incident mitigated when impact is contained, then resolved when the underlying issue is fixed. Confirm recovery with the same monitoring that detected the problem.


**Rootly example:**[Rootly AI SRE](https://docs.rootly.com/ai/ai-sre/overview) investigates alerts and incidents, tests likely causes against evidence from your connected tools, and reports the most likely root cause, while the Rootly lifecycle records mitigated and resolved times separately.


## Phase 4: Communicate


### 12. Publish customer updates on a fixed cadence


**Why it matters:** Silence followed by a long apology costs more trust than a short update every 30 minutes. The[incident communications guide](https://rootly.com/incident-communications) has templates for each stage.


**How to do it:** Decide which severities publish to the status page automatically. Post the first update within minutes of confirming impact, then on a fixed cadence until resolution, even when nothing has changed.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[status pages](https://docs.rootly.com/configuration/status-pages) are built from components, groups and updates (incident, scheduled maintenance), and workflow conditions on severity decide when an incident publishes.


### 13. Notify stakeholders by severity, not by request


**Why it matters:** When leadership and support have to ask for status, they DM responders, and the fix slows down.


**How to do it:** Map each severity to the audiences that need to know: leadership, support, account teams. Send them updates through one announcement channel or email list, owned by the communications lead.


**Rootly example:** Each Rootly severity can carry notify emails and announcement channels, which workflows use to send severity-tiered stakeholder updates automatically.


### 14. Keep one source of truth and brief late joiners automatically


**Why it matters:** Duplicate work during outages usually starts with someone who joined late and repeated a check that was already done.


**How to do it:** Keep the timeline in the incident channel, record the incident bridge call, and give every new joiner a summary before they start working.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[AI summaries](https://docs.rootly.com/ai/ai-summaries) post an incident summary with` /rootly summary` and send a private catchup to responders joining midstream with` /rootly catchup` .[Meeting Scribe](https://docs.rootly.com/ai/meeting-scribe) records and transcribes incident bridge calls.


## Phase 5: Learn


### 15. Right-size retrospectives by severity


**Why it matters:** A full review for every SEV3 burns out the team, and skipping the review for a SEV1 guarantees a repeat.


**How to do it:** Require a retrospective for every SEV0 to SEV2. Use a lighter process for lower severities. Keep it blameless: focus on contributing factors and process gaps, and separate “what happened” from “who did it.”


**Rootly example:** Rootly[retrospective processes](https://docs.rootly.com/retrospectives/configuring-retrospective-processes) apply by severity, incident type or team, and preferences can make the retrospective mandatory or skipped for matching incidents.


### 16. Draft the retrospective from the incident record


**Why it matters:** A retrospective written from memory a week later loses the details that matter. Starting from the timeline keeps it accurate and fast.


**How to do it:** Use one template across teams so reports stay consistent. Fill the timeline, impact and contributing factors from the incident data, then spend the meeting on learnings. The[incident postmortem template](https://rootly.com/incident-postmortems/template) is a good starting point.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[Retrospectives](https://docs.rootly.com/retrospectives/retrospectives) auto-draft sections such as What Happened, Impact, Contributing Factors and Learnings with Rootly AI, inside a collaborative editor.


### 17. Track every action item to done


**Why it matters:** A retrospective without follow-through is theater. Recurring incidents usually trace back to an action item that never closed.


**How to do it:** Give every action item an owner and a due date, put it in the backlog engineers already use, and review overdue items every week.


**Rootly example:** Rootly[action item workflows](https://docs.rootly.com/workflows/action-item-workflows) create or update Jira issues when an action item is created or completed, and notify owners when work is assigned, completed or overdue.


### 18. Measure the process and review it monthly


**Why it matters:** Without numbers, you can’t tell whether a process change helped. The[incident response metrics](https://rootly.com/incident-response/metrics) guide defines each one.


**How to do it:** Track MTTA, MTTR, recurrence rate, retrospective completion, action-item closure and responder load. Review them by severity each month and change one thing at a time.


**Rootly example:** Every Rootly workspace ships with three[default dashboards](https://docs.rootly.com/metrics/default-metrics) (Incident Response, Workload and On-Call Metrics), and the[On-Call Metrics](https://docs.rootly.com/on-call/on-call-metrics) dashboard reports MTTA, MTTR and acknowledge rate.


## Incident management maturity model


Use this table to place your team, then pick the next column over as your goal. Most teams move one level at a time.


Dimension Ad hoc Defined Automated AI-assisted


Declaration and severity Whoever notices posts in a shared channel; severity is a guess Written severity scale; anyone can declare Declaring sets severity and starts that severity’s workflows AI drafts the title and summary from the alert and incident data


Roles Whoever is loudest leads Named commander, comms lead and technical lead Roles assigned by workflow at declaration AI answers “who’s the commander?” and briefs new joiners


Alerting Every monitor pages someone Alerts routed by owner with escalation Alerts grouped and deduplicated before paging AI investigates the alert and reports a likely cause

In Rootly, the Automated column is configuration: severities, workflows, alert routes and retrospective processes. The AI-assisted column uses Rootly AI SRE, AI summaries and Meeting Scribe.


## Incident management best practices checklist


**Prepare**


- Severity scale of four or five levels, each with a written response
- Commander, communications lead and technical lead defined, one line each
- Runbooks for the three to five services that page most
- Every service has an owner and an escalation policy with at least two steps


**Detect**


- Repeat alerts deduplicated and related alerts grouped
- Alerts routed by service ownership on stable fields
- Anyone can declare; uncertain signals start in triage


**Respond**


- One channel per incident, created automatically
- Setup steps (channel, roles, tickets, pages) run by workflow
- Commander coordinates only and hands off out loud
- Mitigate first; record mitigated and resolved times separately


**Communicate**


- Status page updates on a fixed cadence for customer-facing severities
- Stakeholders notified by severity through one channel
- Late joiners get a summary before they start work


**Learn**


- Retrospective required for SEV0 to SEV2, drafted from the incident record
- Every action item has an owner, a due date and a ticket
- MTTA, MTTR, recurrence and action-item closure reviewed monthly


## What is the best way to manage incidents from alert to resolution?


Connect each step so nothing depends on someone remembering it: the alert is grouped and routed to the service owner, an escalation policy pages until someone acknowledges, declaring the incident opens a channel and assigns roles, and status updates go out by severity until resolution. Rootly runs that chain in one platform, from alert routing and on-call through the incident channel, status page and retrospective. The practices above map to each step.


## How can we reduce downtime caused by slow incident coordination?


Automate the first ten minutes. Most coordination delay is setup: finding the owner, opening a channel, deciding who leads and telling stakeholders. Route alerts by ownership, assign roles at declaration, run the incident in one channel, and send stakeholder updates by severity. In Rootly, incident workflows do those steps when the incident is declared, so responders start on diagnosis instead of logistics.


## How do we make sure the right people join an incident quickly?


Page by service ownership instead of by person, and let severity decide who else is invited. Keep a service catalog with an owning team and an escalation policy for every service, so an unacknowledged page escalates by itself. In Rootly, alert routes page the owning team’s escalation policy, and each severity’s linked Slack channels and user groups are invited when the severity is set.


## What should a startup do when incident response is becoming too chaotic?


Put a lightweight, repeatable process in place before the next big incident, and let tooling run the setup so your small team isn’t rebuilding it each time. Rootly does this for startups in Slack or Microsoft Teams: declaring an incident opens the channel, sets severity, assigns roles and pulls in the right responders automatically. Chaos at a startup usually means three things are missing: nobody knows who is in charge, nobody agrees how bad it is, and every incident is handled from scratch.


Fix those in order, and keep each step small enough that a team of ten will follow it:


1. **Name three temporary roles for every incident.** An incident commander coordinates and makes the calls. A scribe keeps a running timeline of events, decisions and actions. Subject-matter experts investigate and fix. On a small team one person may hold two roles, but the commander should not also be the one debugging.
2. **Start with three severity levels.** SEV1: a core service is down, customer data is at risk, or revenue is directly affected, and everyone relevant responds now. SEV2: a key feature is broken or badly degraded for many users. SEV3: a minor bug, a small group of users, or an internal tool, with a workaround. Add levels later if you need them.
3. **Write runbooks for your three to five most critical services first.** Cover the alerts that actually fire, with the diagnostic steps and the fix. Don’t try to document everything at once.
4. **Run every incident in one channel.** A new channel per incident keeps decisions, updates and the timeline in one place, and gives late joiners something to read instead of questions to ask.
5. **Hold a short retrospective after every SEV1 and SEV2.** Keep it blameless, and end with owned, dated action items.


Start with a process that is good enough and that everyone follows, then improve it with each retrospective. A heavy process copied from a large company creates more friction than it removes at your size.

## How can an SRE team avoid confusion over incident roles and ownership?


Assign roles when the incident is declared, route pages by service ownership, and write down what each role does and doesn’t do. Rootly handles the first two automatically: declaring an incident assigns roles, and alerts route to the team and escalation policy that owns the affected service. Confusion comes from roles being claimed informally in the channel, from pages going to whoever set up an alert years ago, and from nobody knowing when the commander has handed off.


- **Assign roles at declaration.** Incident commander, communications lead and a technical lead for each affected service, before anyone starts investigating.
- **Keep ownership in a service catalog.** When every service has an owning team and an escalation policy, the page reaches the right person without anyone guessing.
- **Write one line per role.** The commander coordinates and decides, the communications lead owns every update, and technical leads investigate. A role description that fits on a card is one people will follow under pressure.
- **Hand off out loud.** When the commander changes on a long incident, say so in the channel, so there is never a question about who is in charge.


## Metrics that matter


- **MTTA (mean time to acknowledge):** how fast the right person engages; a proxy for alerting and on-call health.
- **MTTR (mean time to resolve):** the headline speed metric, driven by coordination and automation.
- **Incident recurrence rate:** whether the same failures come back, which tests whether learning sticks.
- **Retrospective completion and action-item closure:** the health of your learning loop.
- **Responder load and[on-call health](https://oncallhealth.ai/) :** a leading indicator of burnout and attrition.


See[incident response metrics](https://rootly.com/incident-response/metrics) for definitions and formulas.


## Common incident management pitfalls


- **Undefined severities:** inconsistent response and slow escalation.
- **Alert overload:** real signals lost in noise.
- **Tool sprawl:** responders juggling dashboards, chat and tickets mid-incident.
- **Manual communication:** updates competing with the fix for responder attention.
- **Retrospectives without follow-up:** the same incidents, forever.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are incident management best practices?


Define severity levels, roles and runbooks before incidents happen; group alerts and route them by service ownership; run each incident in one channel with a named commander; update stakeholders on a fixed cadence; and close every retrospective with tracked action items. Rootly automates most of these steps from Slack, Microsoft Teams or Google Chat.


### What are the core phases of incident management?


Prepare, detect, respond, communicate and learn. Triage happens inside detection and resolution inside response. Strong teams treat it as a loop: lessons from the retrospective feed back into preparation.


### What are incident management best practices for SaaS companies?


Define severity by customer impact, assign roles automatically, run incidents where your team already works, keep customers informed through a status page on a fixed cadence, and close every retrospective with owned action items. Rootly runs each of these from Slack or Microsoft Teams.


### What should a reliability team use to manage incidents and follow-up work?


An incident management platform that covers on-call, the incident channel, status pages and retrospectives, and syncs action items to the tracker engineers already use. Rootly does this in one platform, with action item workflows that create and update Jira issues so follow-up work stays visible until it closes.


### What is the best way to run incident command for software outages?


Name one incident commander per incident whose only job is to coordinate, set severity and make decisions. Give the communications lead every update and the technical leads the investigation. Announce handoffs in the channel. In Rootly, workflows can assign the commander by severity or team on-call, and the timeline records each role change.


### How can incident response teams avoid duplicate work during outages?


Assign each workstream to a named owner, keep every decision in the incident channel, and brief late joiners before they start. Grouping related alerts into one incident also stops two teams from working the same problem. Rootly groups related alerts into one leader alert and sends a private catchup to responders who join midstream.


### How can we create a single source of truth during production incidents?


Run each incident in its own channel, keep the timeline there, and publish external updates from the same record. In Rootly, the incident channel, timeline, status page updates and retrospective all draw on one incident record.


### What should we do if our incident reports are inconsistent across teams?


Use one retrospective template and one severity scale across teams, and draft each report from the incident record instead of memory. Rootly applies retrospective processes by severity, team or incident type and drafts sections such as Impact and Contributing Factors with Rootly AI.


### What is a blameless retrospective?


A retrospective that focuses on systemic and process causes rather than individual fault, so teams surface the truth and fix root causes instead of hiding mistakes.


### How do you reduce MTTR?


Cut alert noise, mobilize the right people automatically, coordinate in one place (Slack, Microsoft Teams or Google Chat), automate communication, and close retrospective action items so incidents don’t recur.


### Who should be involved in an incident?


At minimum an incident commander, a communications lead, and the subject-matter responders for the affected systems, with roles assigned as early as possible.


### What incident management metrics should we track?


MTTA, MTTR, incident recurrence rate, retrospective completion and action-item closure, and on-call responder load.


### What should a startup do when incident response is becoming too chaotic?


Name an incident commander, a scribe and subject-matter experts for every incident, start with three severity levels, write runbooks for your three to five most critical services, and run each incident in its own channel. Rootly automates the setup in Slack or Microsoft Teams, so declaring an incident opens the channel, sets severity and assigns roles.


### How can engineering teams create a repeatable incident management process?


Standardize the first steps so they happen the same way every time: declaration, roles, severity, channel and the first status update. Automate those steps in your incident platform, and use each retrospective to adjust the process rather than rewriting it. Rootly’s workflows run those first steps automatically when an incident is declared.
